title: H5N1 bird flu reaches Australia's wildlife

charter.in: The arrival and spread of H5N1 bird flu in Australia, first confirmed in two migratory seabirds in Western Australia in June 2026. Stories on detections, outbreak events and species affected in Australia (birds, Australian sea lions), and on Australia's wildlife and preparedness response, belong.
out: H5N1 die-offs elsewhere, such as southern elephant seals on South Georgia
The global H5N1 panzootic in general (host-range counts, viral evolution) unless tied to Australia
Migratory bird and seabird declines from other causes (flyway reports, bird population surveys)
Australia's biodiversity policy and threatened species in general
Penguin declines from other causes (African penguins, Antarctic tourism)
charter.endEvent: Australian authorities declare the H5N1 incursion over (the virus no longer detected and the emergency response stood down). If H5N1 instead becomes established in Australian wildlife, no single story ends it and the development stays open.

nearMisses.title: Bird flu killed 53,000 elephant seals on South Georgia
nearMisses.why: The most tempting: H5N1 killing wildlife in the southern oceans, but the deaths are on South Georgia, in the South Atlantic, and date to 2025 or earlier ('by 2025'); the story never mentions Australia.

notes: Not closed: the virus is still spreading in our latest story (9 Oct), and no story reports the incursion declared over. The elephant-seal story (12 Nov) is a different place and development. It reports H5N1 deaths of 53,000 female southern elephant seals on South Georgia 'by 2025', the global decline and the IUCN downgrade, with no reference to Australia. Joining it would merge the southern-hemisphere seal die-off with Australia's incursion. Figures are []: the only numbers in 3 entries are worldwide host-range counts, which describe the global panzootic, not this development, and do not agree with each other. 26 Jun has '560+ wild bird species and over 100 mammal species', 15 Aug 'over 400 bird species and 100 mammal species', and 9 Oct '613 bird types and 112 mammal species worldwide'. Australian numbers appear once each: 'two migratory seabirds' (26 Jun) and 'about 690 reported outbreak events' by 6 October (9 Oct), so they are statuses, not figures. All three entries agree that June 2026 was the first detection ('for the first time' on 26 Jun; 'reached Australia in June, the last continent previously free of the strain' on 9 Oct).
